title: Your Underarms Are Skin. We Formulated BPM That Way.
content:
Deodorant has one obvious job: control odour.

But your underarms are still skin, and we think what you put there every day should take that into account.

That’s why a big part of BPM’s formula isn’t just about fighting odour. It’s built around three ingredients we like for the way they feel on skin: fractionated coconut oil, sunflower seed oil and natural vitamin E.

Fractionated Coconut Oil: The Foundation

Fractionated coconut oil is the dominant ingredient in BPM.

You’ll see it on the ingredient list as Caprylic/Capric Triglyceride, which sounds considerably more intimidating than it is. It’s a lightweight oil made from fatty acids derived from coconut oil.

Its job is partly practical: it gives BPM its smooth glide and helps the cream spread easily without feeling heavy or waxy.

But it’s also an emollient. Emollients help soften and smooth the outer layer of skin by filling the tiny spaces between dry skin cells and leaving behind a light protective film. That can also help reduce moisture loss from the skin.

In other words, it earns its place twice: better application and better skin feel.

Sunflower Oil: More Than a Carrier Oil

Our refined sunflower seed oil brings another layer to the formula.

The sunflower oil we use is naturally rich in linoleic acid, with linoleic acid making up the majority of its measured fatty-acid profile. 

That matters because linoleic acid is an important fatty acid associated with the lipids that make up the skin’s natural moisture barrier.

Sunflower oil also works as an emollient, helping leave skin feeling softer and more conditioned. In a part of the body that deals with shaving, friction, sweat and daily deodorant application, we think that’s worth considering.

Vitamin E: Our Favourite Ingredient

Then there’s tocopherol, better known as vitamin E.

This might be our favourite ingredient in the whole formula.

The natural mixed tocopherol we use is thick, dark amber and almost honey-like. And we use a generous amount of it, not just enough to make “vitamin E” look good on an ingredient story. Our specification calls for a high-purity natural mixed tocopherol rather than diluted vitamin E oil or tocopheryl acetate. 

Vitamin E is a lipid-soluble antioxidant. In simple terms, antioxidants help protect lipids from oxidation. That makes tocopherol useful both inside the formula, where it helps protect the oils, and as a skin-conditioning ingredient when BPM is applied.

Balance Matters

BPM isn’t trying to be an underarm moisturizer disguised as deodorant.

The conditioning oils are balanced with ingredients such as tapioca starch and kaolin that absorb excess oil and moisture, alongside magnesium hydroxide and zinc ricinoleate for odour control. The result is meant to feel smooth and conditioned, not oily.

That balance is intentional.

Serious odour control. Skin-conditioning oils. Natural vitamin E.

Because deodorant has a job to do. But the skin underneath it matters too.
summary:
Your underarms are skin too. BPM is built with skin-conditioning fractionated coconut oil, linoleic-rich sunflower oil, and natural vitamin E to help leave skin soft, smooth and comfortable.

title: The Name Behind BPM: Indigenous Ownership and Finding My Way Back
content:
I want to share something about BPM that we have not talked about publicly in much detail.

Bold Egg Naturals, the company behind BPM Deodorant, is a Certified Indigenous Business through the Canadian Council for Indigenous Business. I am a registered member of the Algonquins of Pikwàkanagàn First Nation, and my family’s original name is Kohoko, which means owl.

I know I may not look like what some people picture when they hear “Indigenous.”

I look like my father, who was Lithuanian and Irish. My mother, who is Algonquin, raised me on her own in Toronto. My parents were never married, and after my father died, my surname was changed to his. So I carry the name and much of the appearance of a man I did not grow up with, along with the heritage of the mother who actually raised me.

Indigenous people come in every appearance you can imagine. There is no single look. Families like mine are part of that story.

I also did not grow up closely connected to my community. That is something I have struggled with more as I have grown older.

There are many reasons Indigenous people grow up disconnected. Some are personal. Others reach back through residential schools, the child welfare system, adoption and government policies that separated families and interrupted the passing down of language, culture and community. Those effects do not stop with one generation.

For most of my life, being Algonquin was something I knew about myself, but not something I knew how to live inside. I knew where my mother came from. I knew our family name. But I did not grow up with a strong relationship to Pikwàkanagàn, and I was never quite sure what to do with that distance.

My career took me in a completely different direction. I spent years in technology and product management before moving into investment and eventually starting Bold Egg Naturals.

BPM did not begin as a heritage project. It began because I wanted to make a better deodorant. Something natural that worked, used less wasteful packaging and did not come with an inflated price. I built it through formulation work, packaging problems, testing, mistakes and a lot of persistence.

But as BPM became a real business, it also gave me an opportunity to bring forward a part of myself that I had mostly left in the background.

Getting the company certified through the Canadian Council for Indigenous Business meant more to me than putting a badge on a website. The certification confirmed that BPM is majority Indigenous owned and controlled. On paper, that is straightforward. Personally, it meant putting my family history on the table and saying openly that this is part of who I am.

It became a small but concrete way to reconnect.

Indigenous ownership does not mean that I have built BPM around cultural imagery or teachings I did not grow up with. It means something simpler and more tangible. It means an Indigenous person owns this company, makes its decisions and benefits from the value it creates. When BPM grows, an Indigenous owned Canadian business grows with it.

It also means that building BPM has become part of my own unfinished relationship with where I come from.

I do not have a neat ending to that story. I am a registered member of my Nation, but I am still figuring out what connection looks like for me. Building a business does not resolve that distance. It has simply given me a place to begin acknowledging it instead of leaving it unspoken.

There are probably more people in a similar position than most of us realize. People who know their history but did not grow up immersed in it. People who do not fit the expected picture. People finding their own way back, sometimes much later in life.

So when you see the Indigenous owned badge on our website, this is the story behind it.

BPM is the name customers know. Kohoko is the family name that came before it.

Both are now part of what I am building.

Thank you for being part of it.

Corey Goss
Founder, BPM Natural Deodorant
summary:
Behind BPM’s Indigenous-owned badge is a personal story about family, identity and reconnection. Founder Corey Goss shares his Algonquin roots, the meaning behind the family name Kohoko, and why building BPM became about more than deodorant.

title: The Math Behind Fair Pricing: BPM vs Native vs Schmidt's
content:
One of BPM's founding pillars is making natural products, priced fairly and transparently. BPM's tube packaging was chosen specifically to support that: precise, thin dispensing wastes almost nothing. Here is what that actually costs per use, in real Canadian dollars, not marketing math.

A pea sized dab covers one underarm, so a full daily application, both underarms, uses two dabs. A 76 gram BPM tube holds about 304 pea sized dabs, which works out to about 152 full daily applications, or roughly 5 months of daily use.

Product Regular price (CAD) Full daily applications Cost per use
BPM tube, 76 g $23.99 152 $0.16
Schmidt's stick, 75 g $11.08 (avg) ~75* $0.15
Native stick, 75 g $18.32 (avg) 92* $0.20

Measured this way, BPM costs about 21 percent less per use than Native, and is essentially on par with Schmidt's, running about 7 percent higher per use. We are not going to round that away. What the tube still does better, measurably, is use less product to get there: about half a gram per full application versus about a gram for a stick swipe. That is the entire reason a $23.99 tube, at a higher price per gram than either competitor, still lasts about 5 months of daily use, twice as long as Schmidt's roughly 2.5 months, and well past Native's roughly 3 months.

On a monthly basis, that works out to about $4.73 for BPM, $4.43 for Schmidt's, and $5.97 for Native. BPM and Schmidt's land within about 30 cents of each other a month. Native still costs noticeably more, about $1.24 more a month than BPM and about $1.54 more than Schmidt's.

I am genuinely proud of where we are priced right now. We are a small batch, handmade product, and we are already on par per application with brands that have decades of manufacturing scale behind them.

- Corey Goss, Founder, BPM Natural Deodorant

There is context worth putting next to that near tie with Schmidt's. Schmidt's is a large, established brand running high volume manufacturing. BPM is made in small batches, by hand. Landing within 7 percent of an established competitor's cost per use, before BPM has any of the manufacturing scale that competitor has, is where we are starting from, not where we plan to stay. We expect that gap to close, and possibly reverse, as our own production scales up.

Prices are the average regular, non sale price found at three Canadian retailers per brand (Walmart Canada, Well.ca, and Healthy Planet Canada), specifically excluding rollback and flash sale prices so the comparison reflects what customers actually pay most of the year, not a one day discount. Schmidt's application count comes from Schmidt's own stated 3 month stick life. *Native publishes no duration or application count anywhere we could find, so we tested it ourselves. Corey personally counted applications from a purchased Native stick, both underarms per application, on camera from first use to empty, and recorded 92. That is our own first party test, not a Native claim, and we have the video to back it up.

"Fair and transparent pricing means showing customers the real math, even the part where we are not the cheapest option on the shelf," says Corey Goss, Founder and President of BPM Natural Deodorant. "I am genuinely proud of where we are priced right now. We are a small batch, handmade product, and we are already on par per application with brands that have decades of manufacturing scale behind them. We still have a lot of optimizing left to do on our end, and as we scale, I expect our prices to come down, not up."

summary:
We ran the real math on cost per use for BPM Natural Deodorant against Native and Schmidt's, using sourced Canadian pricing, no rounding in our favor.

title: Deodorant Is Changing Shape. Here's Why We Chose Cream.
content:
For decades, deodorant came in two familiar forms: a stick or a spray. Walk into a major retailer now and the shelf looks very different.

Gels. Creams. Mists. Whole-body deodorants. Products made for feet, thighs, skin folds and other high-sweat areas, not just underarms.

Deodorant hasn't suddenly forgotten what it is. It's finally catching up with how people actually use it.

Why the Category Is Expanding

Traditional antiperspirants were built around one primary job: reducing underarm sweat. Their format followed that purpose. A solid stick delivered aluminum compounds directly to the underarm, while aerosols sprayed them over a wider area.

The growth of aluminum-free and whole-body deodorants has widened the category beyond traditional sweat prevention. When the goal is controlling odour rather than reducing perspiration, brands have more freedom to rethink where deodorant is used and what form it takes.

Odour doesn't happen only under your arms. Neither does friction, moisture or skin sensitivity. Creams and gels can be applied precisely to different external areas, while sprays make it easier to cover larger ones.

Consumers are also paying closer attention to ingredients and skin comfort. They want products that feel more like skincare: easy to spread, gentle on sensitive areas and available in unscented or baking-soda-free options.

The result is more choice, but also more confusion. A product labelled “whole body” may be a cream, spray or stick, and each format behaves differently. Format is no longer just a packaging decision. It affects where the product can go, how much you use and what has to be added to make it work.

Why BPM Is a Cream

We chose a cream because it gives you control.

A small amount can be spread thinly and widely, exactly where it's needed. There's no rigid stick dragging across the skin, no propellant carrying product into the air and no need to force the formula into a shape it doesn't naturally want to hold.

That last part mattered to us.

Producing a conventional solid stick would have required additional structuring ingredients, typically waxes or similar materials, whose main job would be keeping the product firm inside its container. We didn't want to add ingredients simply to satisfy a familiar format.

Instead, we built the formula around performance. Magnesium hydroxide and zinc ricinoleate address odour. Tapioca starch and kaolin help manage moisture. Lightweight oils give the cream glide and allow it to spread evenly.

Every ingredient has a job.

The cream works for underarms, but it isn't trapped there. It can also be applied to appropriate external high-sweat areas where a conventional stick would be awkward or imprecise. You decide where it goes and how much you need.

It is also concentrated. Start with a pea-sized amount, spread it thinly and let the formula do the work. More product doesn't mean more protection.

The Packaging Shaped the Format Too

We considered paperboard packaging, but it didn't meet our standard for durability. Deodorant lives in humid bathrooms, gets handled with damp hands and gets crushed inside gym bags and luggage. Paper can soften, ripple and lose its shape in exactly those conditions.

We explain that decision more fully in What's Changing in Deodorant Packaging Right Now (and Why We Went With Metal).

Metal gave us the durability and recyclability we wanted without requiring a complicated plastic dispensing mechanism. A collapsible tube also works naturally with a cream formula.

That connection matters: we didn't develop a formula and then find something to put it in. The formula, format and packaging were designed to work together.

Choosing cream meant we could use a durable metal tube. Choosing the tube meant we didn't have to add extra ingredients just to create a solid stick.

The Stick Isn't Disappearing

Sticks and sprays will remain popular because they're familiar and convenient. What's changing is the assumption that they're the only forms deodorant should take.

The category is moving away from one product, one body part and one method of application. That means more useful options for different bodies, routines and skin types.

BPM chose cream because it gave us the most direct route to the product we wanted to make: concentrated, adaptable, wax-free and packaged to withstand real life.

Nothing extra. Everything intentional.

Try BPM in Bergamot & Lime or Unscented — or browse all natural deodorants.
summary:
Deodorant is expanding beyond the stick and spray and the reasons go deeper than trend. This post explores why the category is shifting toward creams, gels and whole-body formats, and the specific decisions behind BPM's cream formula: no waxes, no unnecessary structuring ingredients, and packaging designed to work with the formula rather than around it.

title: What's Changing in Deodorant Packaging Right Now (and Why We Went With Metal)
content:
Deodorant packaging is having a moment. Not the product inside the tube — the tube itself.

For years, the format barely changed: a plastic stick, twist up from the bottom, toss it when it's empty. That's starting to shift, fast. Brands are moving to paperboard tubes, compostable push-up sticks, refill pods, glass jars. Some of that is genuine innovation. Some of it is a plastic problem finally catching up with an industry that's been packaging deodorant the same way since the 1950s.

Why now

A few things are pushing this at once.

Regulation is catching up. Europe's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation is pushing brands toward less plastic and more reuse, and it's shaping what gets manufactured well beyond the EU. When a regulation that size moves, packaging suppliers move with it.

Plastic recycling was never as good as the label implied. Most curbside programs can't actually process the mixed-material tubes deodorant has shipped in for decades — cap, barrel, and liner are often different plastics fused together, which makes them close to unrecyclable in practice even when the label says otherwise. That's finally becoming common knowledge instead of fine print.

Refillable is turning from a nice-to-have into an expectation. Consumer interest in refill systems has climbed fast enough that it's stopped being a sustainability footnote and started being something brands compete on.

The result: a lot of new deodorant packaging right now, and not all of it built for the job.

Why we didn't go paper

Paperboard tubes are having a real moment, and we get the appeal. They feel light, they feel green, they're an easy swap from plastic. But cardboard and moisture don't mix well, and a deodorant tube spends its whole life in a humid bathroom getting handled with damp hands. Paper tubes can soften, lose their shape, and get less hygienic over time in exactly the environment they're used in. That's a real trade-off, not a minor one and it's not one we were willing to make just to check the "sustainable" box.

Toss a paperboard tube in a toiletry bag and you've got a second problem. It's not built for getting jammed between a phone charger and a pair of shoes. Corners crush, seams split, the whole thing gets soft and dented before it's even halfway used. A deodorant that can't survive a carry-on isn't actually solving anything for the person using it daily.

Why metal

Metal solves the problem paper can't: it doesn't care about humidity. Non-porous, doesn't soften, doesn't interact with what's inside it the way some plastics can over time. It holds its shape and holds the formula, full stop.

It also survives being thrown in a bag. Metal takes a beating and keeps its shape — no dents that turn into rips, no soft spots from getting tossed around next to your other toiletries. If you're the kind of person who packs for a trip and doesn't think twice about where the deodorant lands, that's the tube built for you.

It's also genuinely recyclable — not "technically recyclable if your city has the right facility," but aluminum specifically, which is one of the few materials that can be recycled indefinitely without losing quality. That's a real end-of-life story, not a marketing one.

And it looks like what it is: minimal, durable, no wasted material. That's the whole BPM philosophy in a tube. Nothing extra, everything intentional. A recyclable metal tube isn't a trend we jumped on. It's just the option that didn't ask us to trade performance for a good story.

Try BPM in Bergamot & Lime or Unscented — or shop all natural deodorants.

The bottom line

Packaging is changing because the industry finally has to reckon with a few decades of plastic it can't actually recycle. Some of the new options are real progress. Some are a different kind of waste wearing a green label. We picked metal because it does the job, keeps the formula stable, holds up in a bathroom, and actually gets recycled when you're done with it, without asking you to trust a claim you can't verify.
summary:
Deodorant packaging is shifting away from plastic and paper isn't the fix people think it is. Here's why we picked metal instead.

title: How to Switch to Natural Deodorant (Without the Awkward Transition Period)
content:
If you've used conventional antiperspirant for years, your body has adapted to it. Antiperspirants work by physically plugging your sweat ducts with aluminum compounds,  stopping something your body is built to do. Stop using them, and your body needs time to adjust. That window is usually somewhere between one and four weeks, and it varies person to person.

During that stretch, you might notice: 

  • More sweating than usual, as the ducts that were plugged open back up
  • Odour that's stronger or different than what you're used to, as your skin's bacteria rebalance
  • Some underarm sensitivity

None of that means the deodorant isn't working. It means your body's doing exactly what it's supposed to do once you take the plug out.

Making the Switch Easier

1. Time it right. Start during a lower-pressure stretch if you can such as a slower week, a break from the gym, whatever gives your body room to adjust without a big presentation riding on it.

2. Stay consistent. Apply every morning, even on days you don't think you need it. Consistency is what gets your underarm bacteria to settle faster.

3. Keep things clean. Wash daily with a gentle, pH-balanced cleanser. It clears out odour-causing bacteria without stripping your skin, which makes the whole adjustment period shorter and easier.

4. Reapply if you need to. In the first couple of weeks, a midday touch-up on a high-activity day is normal. It doesn't mean the formula's failing you.

5. Start with the right formula. If your skin runs sensitive, a baking soda-free formula from day one makes the whole thing easier. Irritated skin and a thrown-off pH just slow everything down.

What to Expect

Most people are through the adjustment within one to four weeks with some faster, some slower. Sweat and odour tend to be most noticeable early on and settle as your body catches up. If you're still uncomfortable well past the month mark, that's worth a closer look at the formula, not something to push through.

A Note on Sweating

Natural deodorant doesn't stop you from sweating, and that's the point. Sweating is how your body regulates temperature. It's not something to block, it's something to work with. A good natural deodorant neutralizes odour. It doesn't shut down a system your body needs.

BPM uses magnesium hydroxide and tapioca starch to absorb moisture and neutralize odour, without interfering with what your body's actually trying to do. Browse the full Natural Deodorant collection to find your fit.

You Won't Want to Go Back

The adjustment period can feel discouraging in the moment. Most people who push through it land somewhere better with less irritation, and the simple upside of knowing exactly what's in the tube.
summary:
Switching to natural deodorant can come with a transition period. Here's exactly what to expect and how to make it as smooth as possible.

title: Best Natural Deodorant for Sensitive Skin: What to Look For (and What to Avoid)
content:
Your underarm is thin-skinned, gets rubbed by clothing all day, and takes a razor to it regularly. It doesn't take much to tip that into irritated. Pair it with the wrong deodorant and you've got redness, itching, and a reason to dread applying it.

Here's the part people don't expect: a well-formulated natural deodorant can be gentler than a conventional antiperspirant. Not automatically. Only if it's actually built for the job. Here's what that means in practice.

What to Skip

  • Baking soda — pH of 8–9 against your skin's natural 4.5–5.5. That gap is what disrupts your acid mantle and shows up as redness, burning, and, with repeated irritation, darker patches over time.
  • Aluminum compounds — plug sweat ducts to stop wetness. Effective at what they do, but that same mechanism can irritate sensitive skin.
  • Synthetic fragrance — one of the most common triggers for contact dermatitis, full stop. If it's scented, the scent should come from essential oils, not a fragrance blend.
  • Alcohol — dries skin out, especially right after shaving.
  • Parabens — can trigger reactions in skin that's already prone to them.

What Actually Works

  • Odour fighters. The active ingredient doing the real work, neutralizing the bacteria that cause smell in the first place. Zinc ricinoleate is one option, working quietly to bind odour molecules rather than mask them. Magnesium hydroxide is another common choice, worth a note here, since it gets marketed as "gentler" for a reason people usually get wrong. It's not gentler because it's closer to your skin's pH; it's actually more alkaline than baking soda on paper. It's gentler because it dissolves slowly in sweat and releases gradually, instead of hitting your skin with a sharp pH spike all at once.
  • Plant-based oils. These condition the skin instead of stripping it, and give the formula something to glide on rather than drag. Coconut oil is a common pick for its light texture and skin-conditioning properties. Sunflower oil is another rich in vitamin E and fatty acids that help support the skin barrier rather than work against it.
  • Absorbent powders. This is what keeps things dry without the grit or the pH spike of baking soda. Tapioca starch is a clean, fine option that absorbs moisture without irritating. Arrowroot does similar work and shows up in a lot of sensitive-skin formulas for the same reason. Kaolin clay is another that is gentle, mineral-based, and good at soaking up moisture without disrupting the skin.

What to Look for Beyond the Ingredient List

  • Baking soda-free. Not negotiable if your skin reacts easily.
  • A short, recognizable ingredient list. Fewer ingredients, fewer chances for something to go wrong.
  • No synthetic fragrance. Scented is fine. Fragrance-from-a-lab isn't.
  • A formula that works with your skin's pH, not against it.

Format Matters Too

  • Metal tubes are non-porous and don't interact with the formula the way some plastics can over time.
  • Sticks are generally gentler than sprays, which rely on propellants that can irritate sensitive skin.
  • Cardboard tubes absorb moisture and get less hygienic the longer they sit in a humid bathroom. Metal holds up better.

BPM checks every one of these boxes: baking soda-free, no synthetic fragrance, short ingredient list, packaged in a recyclable metal tube. Browse our Sensitive Skin Deodorant collection or shop Bergamot & Lime and Unscented directly.

A Note on Patch Testing

Even a gentle formula isn't a guarantee if your skin is highly reactive. Do a 24-hour patch test on your inner arm before switching over fully. Ten minutes of caution beats a week of irritation.
summary:
Not all natural deodorants are gentle. Here's what to look for (and what to avoid) if you have sensitive skin.

title: Is Baking Soda Bad for Sensitive Skin? What You Need to Know
content:
Baking soda has a pH of around 8–9. Your skin sits around 4.5–5.5. That's not a small gap. It's the difference between your skin's protective acid mantle staying intact and getting knocked off balance.

For a lot of people, that imbalance shows up fast:

  • Redness and irritation
  • Burning or stinging
  • Rashes and contact dermatitis
  • Over time, in some cases, patches of darker skin where the irritation kept coming back

Not everyone reacts. Some people wear baking soda deodorant for years without issue. But "some people are fine" isn't the same as "it's fine" and if your skin has ever gone from calm to angry a few days into a new natural deodorant, baking soda is the usual suspect.

Why It's Still Everywhere

Baking soda works. It neutralizes the bacteria that cause odour, it's cheap, and it's easy to source, which is exactly why it became the default in early natural deodorants. None of that makes it a good match for every underarm. It just makes it a convenient one.

What We Use Instead

Ditching baking soda doesn't mean giving up odour protection. It means picking ingredients that do the same job without the same fallout:

  • Magnesium hydroxide — neutralizes odour-causing bacteria the same way baking soda does, but through a slow, steady release instead of a sharp pH spike. It's not a "gentler pH" as magnesium hydroxide is actually more alkaline than baking soda on paper. The difference is timing: it dissolves gradually in sweat instead of hitting your skin all at once, which is why skin that reacts to baking soda often tolerates it fine.
  • Tapioca starch — absorbs moisture and keeps the formula gliding on instead of sitting gritty.
  • Plant-based oils and emulsifiers — condition the skin instead of stripping it.

This is the formula we build BPM around. No baking soda. No aluminum. Zinc and magnesium doing the actual work, nothing extra along for the ride.

Check out our Sensitive Skin Deodorant collection or browse the full Natural Deodorant range.

How to Tell If Baking Soda Is the Problem

If a natural deodorant has left you red, itchy, or burning, baking soda is the most common cause. Reaction timelines vary. For some people it's days, for others it takes longer to build up so don't rule it out just because the first week was fine.

The upside: switching to a baking soda-free formula is usually enough to let skin recover. How long that takes depends on the person and how irritated things got, so we won't put a number on it we can't back up.

Bottom Line

Baking soda isn't dangerous. It's just not built for every underarm, and a lot of "natural deodorant doesn't work for me" stories are really "baking soda doesn't work for me" stories. If yours is one of them, the fix isn't giving up on natural deodorant, it's finding a formula that skips the ingredient causing the problem.
summary:
Baking soda has a high pH that disrupts your skin's natural acid mantle. Here's why it causes irritation and what to use instead.
